questions.question: How does inheritance work at a basic level in Ruby?
questions.title: Inheritance Basics
questions.direct_answer: At its simplest: `class B < A; end` makes B inherit A's methods. When you call b.foo, Ruby looks up b's class (B), then its superclass (A), then Object, etc., until it finds foo — the method lookup chain. B can override A's method (define its own foo); it can call A's version with super. An instance of B is an instance of A too (b.is_a?(A) # true). Constructors are inherited in lookup but usually you redefine initialize and call super with the right args. Class variables (@@x) are shared up the chain (often a surprise). Instance variables (@x) belong to the object, not the class. Inheritance models 'B is a kind of A'. Keep trees shallow; one level is common, two is okay, more gets fragile. Use modules when you want to share behavior without an is-a link.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know method lookup goes up the superclass chain and that B instances are also A instances.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting method lookup walks the chain (or that @@vars are shared up it), or deep trees.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Inheritance basics: class B < A; method lookup walks B -> A -> Object. B overrides A; super calls A. b.is_a?(A). @@vars shared up the chain.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Inheritance Basics simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: class B < A makes B inherit A's methods; method lookup goes B -> A -> Object.
B can override A's method; super calls A's version.
An instance of B is also an instance of A (b.is_a?(A) # true).
Redefine initialize and call super with the right args (constructors aren't auto-called).
@@class vars are shared up the chain (a subclass's change affects the parent).

B can override A's method (define its own foo); it can call A's version with super. An instance of B is an instance of A too (b is_a A true). Constructors are inherited in lookup but usually you redefine initialize and call super with the right args. Class variables (count) are shared up the chain (often a surprise). Instance variables (x) belong to the object, not the class. Inheritance models B is a kind of A. Keep trees shallow; one level is common, two is okay, more gets fragile. Use modules when you want to share behavior without an is-a link. A common mistake is forgetting method lookup walks the chain, and that class vars are shared up it, which is a surprise.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
At its simplest: `class B < A; end` makes B inherit A's methods.

When you call b.foo, Ruby looks up b's class (B), then its superclass (A), then Object, etc., until it finds foo — the method lookup chain.

B can override A's method (define its own foo); it can call A's version with super. An instance of B is an instance of A too (b.is_a?(A) # true). Constructors are inherited in lookup but usually you redefine initialize and call super with the right args. Class variables (@@x) are shared up the chain (often a surprise). Instance variables (@x) belong to the object, not the class. Inheritance models 'B is a kind of A'. Keep trees shallow; one level is common, two is okay, more gets fragile.

A common mistake is forgetting method lookup walks the chain (or that @@vars are shared up it), or deep trees.

sections.title: Inheritance Basics
sections.content:
class B < A; method lookup B -> A -> Object. override + super. b.is_a?(A). @@vars shared up.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[b.foo] --> L1[look in B]
  L1 --> L2[then A]
  L2 --> L3[then Object]
  O[B overrides foo] --> S[super -> A's foo]
```

sections.title: Inheritance basics
sections.content:
```ruby
class A
  def greet; "hello from A"; end
  def name;  'A'; end
end

# B inherits A's methods
class B < A
  def greet                  # override A#greet
    super + " (B too)"       # super -> A#greet
  end
end

b = B.new
b.greet       # 'hello from A (B too)'  (B's greet, called super)
b.name        # 'A'  (inherited from A; not overridden)
b.is_a?(A)   # true  (a B IS an A)
b.is_a?(B)   # true

# METHOD LOOKUP walks the chain: B -> A -> Object -> Kernel -> BasicObject
B.ancestors   # [B, A, Object, Kernel, BasicObject]
# Ruby finds the FIRST method named `greet` going up -> B's greet.

# initialize: usually redefine and call super
class Named
  def initialize(name); @name = name; end
  attr_reader :name
end
class Dog < Named
  def initialize(name, breed)
    super(name)              # pass name to Named#initialize
    @breed = breed
  end
  attr_reader :breed
end
d = Dog.new('Rex', 'Lab')
d.name     # 'Rex'  (set by super -> Named#initialize)
d.breed    # 'Lab'

# @@class vars are SHARED up the chain (surprise!):
class Base; @@count = 0; end
class Sub < Base; @@count = 5; end   # changes Base's @@count too!

# Keep trees SHALLOW; use modules to share behavior without is-a.
```
